title: Blood glucose and hormone levels after a meal

stimulus.title: A model of glucose control, and one meal
stimulus.text: The diagram is a model of how blood glucose is regulated. The graph shows blood glucose (mg/dL), insulin (µU/mL) and glucagon (pg/mL) in a healthy teenager during the 3 hours after a meal rich in carbohydrate, eaten at time 0. Each is plotted in its own unit.
stimulus.html: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" width="100%" style="max-width:760px;height:auto" role="img" aria-labelledby="frqgl-t frqgl-d"> <title id="frqgl-t">Negative feedback loops that hold blood glucose near its set point</title> <desc id="frqgl-d">A box on the left shows blood glucose near its set point, about 70 to 100 milligrams per deciliter when fasting. Top loop: after a meal glucose rises above the range; beta cells in the pancreas sense the rise and release insulin; muscle and fat cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen; glucose falls back to the range. Bottom loop: during fasting or exercise glucose falls below the range; alpha cells in the pancreas sense the fall and release glucagon; the liver breaks down glycogen and releases glucose; glucose rises back to the range. parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the role of the beta cells in the model.

rubric.point: Describes the beta cells as the sensor and control center: they detect the rise in blood glucose and respond by releasing insulin.
accept: they sense high blood glucose and release insulin
beta cells detect the stimulus and send the insulin signal
sensor and control center that secretes insulin when glucose rises

parts.sample: The beta cells act as the sensor and control center of the upper loop. They detect that blood glucose has risen above its normal range and respond by releasing insulin into the blood.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the graph, explain how the data show that glucose is regulated by negative feedback.

rubric.point: Explains that insulin rises as glucose rises (peaking at about 45 minutes) and glucose then falls back to about 85 mg/dL, after which insulin falls too: the response opposes the change and switches off when glucose returns to its set point.
accept: insulin rises after glucose rises, glucose returns to baseline, then insulin returns to baseline
the response (insulin) reverses the rise in glucose and stops when glucose is back to normal
glucose goes up to 140 and back to 85 as insulin goes up to 62 and back to 9

parts.sample: After the meal glucose rises from 85 to 140 mg/dL, and insulin rises with it from 8 to 62 µU/mL. Glucose then falls back to 85 by 180 minutes, and insulin falls back to 9 as glucose returns. The response (insulin and the uptake it causes) opposed the change and switched off once glucose was back near its set point, which is negative feedback.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Glucagon falls after the meal. Using the model, explain why the fall in glucagon helps return blood glucose to its set point.

rubric.point: Explains that glucagon makes the liver break down glycogen and release glucose, so less glucagon means the liver releases less glucose into the blood while glucose is high, helping the level fall.
accept: lower glucagon means less glycogen breakdown and less glucose released by the liver
the liver stops adding glucose to the blood when glucagon is low
less glucagon removes a source of glucose that would oppose insulin

parts.sample: In the model, glucagon makes the liver break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. When glucose is high after the meal, glucagon falls from 90 to 70 pg/mL, so the liver adds less glucose to the blood. With less glucose coming in while insulin drives glucose out, the level falls back toward its set point faster.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In type 2 diabetes, muscle and fat cells respond weakly to insulin. Predict how the glucose and insulin curves after the same meal would differ from those shown. Justify your prediction using the model.

rubric.point: Predicts that glucose rises higher and stays high longer, and insulin rises higher (and stays higher), because the effectors take up glucose poorly, so the stimulus (high glucose) persists and the beta cells keep releasing insulin.
accept: glucose peaks higher and falls slowly; insulin is higher because high glucose keeps stimulating the beta cells
higher, longer glucose and higher insulin because the response does not remove the stimulus
both curves end up higher than the healthy ones

parts.sample: Glucose would rise higher than 140 mg/dL and take much longer to return to 85, and insulin would rise higher than 62 µU/mL and stay high. In the model, insulin lowers glucose only through the effectors, muscle and fat cells taking up glucose. If they respond weakly, glucose is removed slowly, so the stimulus stays, and the beta cells keep releasing more insulin.
